chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Al-Fadl ibn Shazan, all from Safwan ibn Yahya, and Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muawiya ibn Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

When you enter the Sacred Masjid, enter it barefoot, with tranquility, dignity, and reverence. And he (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever enters it with reverence, Allah will forgive him, if Allah wills.' I said, 'What is the reverence?' He (peace be upon him) said, 'Tranquility; do not enter it with arrogance.'

So when you reach the door of the Masjid, stand and say: 'Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings. In the name of Allah, and by Allah, and from Allah, and whatever Allah willed. And peace be upon the prophets of Allah and His messengers. And peace be upon the Messenger of Allah, and peace be upon Ibrahim. And praise is to Allah, Lord of the worlds.'

So when you enter the Masjid, raise your hands and face the House (Kaaba) and say: 'O Allah, I ask You in this standing of mine, at the beginning of my rituals, that You accept my repentance, overlook my errors, and remove my burden. Praise is to Allah who brought me to His Sacred House. O Allah, I testify that this is Your Sacred House, which You made a refuge for people, a secure abode, blessed, and a guidance for the worlds.'

O Allah, I am Your servant, the city is Your city, and the House is Your House. I have come seeking Your mercy and intending to obey You, obedient to Your command, pleased with Your decree. I ask You with the asking of the desperate to You, the one fearful of Your punishment. O Allah, open for me the doors of Your mercy, and employ me in Your obedience and pleasure.
ai.seo_question: What are the recommended etiquettes and supplications when entering the Sacred Masjid in Mecca?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi details the specific ritual etiquette (adab) for entering the Masjid al-Haram, emphasizing that true khushu (reverence) is manifested through physical tranquility and the absence of arrogance. It prescribes a structured sequence of greetings to the Prophet, Ibrahim, and the angels, followed by a supplication that acknowledges God’s ownership of the sanctuary, reflecting the Shia tradition of linking physical entry with spiritual submission.
